guide.title: The useful result is not a winning test; it is a repeatable way to choose one for your own metric distribution.
guide.problem: Small CTR differences can be financially meaningful, but random user behaviour can produce differences of the same size even when both ranking variants are identical. A direct comparison therefore confuses sampling noise with a product improvement.
guide.core_idea: Model views and each user’s latent click probability, generate many controlled A/A and A/B experiments, then measure both false-positive rate and sensitivity for T-Test, Mann–Whitney and bucketed variants. Real A/A traffic is used as a final calibration check.
guide.outcome: Different distribution shapes favour different tests. Mann–Whitney performs well in many simulations, while bucketing becomes competitive under more regular ground-truth CTR distributions. The article deliberately avoids presenting one universal statistical test.
takeaways: Start from the unit of independence. Tiki groups observations by user because treating dependent impressions or sessions as independent makes p-values look more certain than they are.
Validate a test with A/A data before trusting its A/B verdict. If the null case already exceeds the accepted false-positive rate, product decisions built on it are unsafe.
Sensitivity and false-positive rate must be evaluated together. A conservative test that never detects a real uplift is not automatically a good test.
Simulation is most useful when its view counts and latent CTRs resemble production. Elegant assumptions that miss the real distribution can select the wrong method.
Bucketing changes the observation unit and weighting behaviour; bucket size is a domain parameter to test, not a magic constant.
review_lenses: Experiment assignment: verify stable user allocation, exclusion rules and independence from concurrent experiments.
Metric definition: specify the denominator, aggregation unit and treatment of users with very little activity.
Power planning: connect minimum detectable effect, sample size and full weekly behaviour before setting duration.
Decision policy: document multiple-testing corrections, guardrail metrics and what happens when statistical and business significance disagree.
